name: The dialectic of feudalism, capitalism, and Socialism (classes replacing nations)
plain_explanation: Marx borrowed Hegel's three-step pattern of historical development but changed its subject: instead of nations acting out a mystical Spirit's logic, it is economic classes (landowners, industrial employers, wage-earners) that move history forward toward Socialism.
precise_definition: Marx's substitution of a single historical triad -- feudalism (the landowner), capitalism (the industrial employer), and Socialism (the wage-earner) -- and of classes for Hegel's nations, as the vehicles of an inevitable, deterministic dialectical movement.
why_it_mattered: It gave Marx's Socialism the appearance of scientific inevitability (a prophecy, not merely an ethical preference), while, Russell argues, quietly smuggling in an unexamined belief in progress that only theism could really justify.
historical_origin: Adapted from Hegel's philosophy of history as expressed in the Logic.
objections: Russell notes Marx disclaimed ethical or humanitarian grounds for preferring Socialism, calling it merely the side taken by the deterministic dialectic -- yet Russell judges this only partly true, since Marx clearly also believed Socialism would increase human happiness.
competing_positions: Hegel's own version, in which 'Spirit,' not matter, drives historical development through nations rather than classes
influence_on_later_thinkers: Shaped the Social Democratic Party's programme in Germany and, in a more fanatical form, the government of Soviet Russia.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political: frames the modern division between Liberals, Marxists, and Fascists/Nazis.
